newsitem.title: SOMALIA: EU envoy meets Somali north Mogadishu leader.
newsitem.headline: EU envoy meets Somali north Mogadishu leader.

text.p: Somali faction leader Ali Mahdi Mohamed held talks with the European Union's special envoy on Saturday on ways to stabilise the country and bring humanitarian aid to drought-stricken areas.
EU Special Envoy Sigurd Illing told reporters he encouraged attempts by local authorities to work towards pacifying Somalia.
He said he Ali Mahdi -- who controls north of the capital Mogadishu -- discussed security and ways to bring humanitarian aid to drought-stricken parts of the country.
Illing's held talks with Mohamed's arch-enemy, south Mogadishu leader Hussein Aideed, on Friday during which they also discussed reconciliation between Somalis.
The special envoy is in Somalia for the first time since the lifting of a nine-month ban on his visiting the country.
Illing was barred by Aideed's late father, Mohamed Farah Aideed, from visiting Somalia last April after he was accused of entering the country illegally and fomenting civil strife.
Hussein Aideed was elected Somalia's president by supporters last August after his father's death but his government only controls part of the country from a south Mogadishu stronghold.
The ban on Illing was lifted on January 20 shortly before a meeting and peace agreement mediated by an Italian envoy between Aideed and Ali Mahdi.

The anarchic Horn of Africa country has been devastated by factional fighting since 1991 when rebels overthrew late president Mohamed Siad Barre and then turned their guns on each other in vicious fighting which killed thousands of people.

Outside the capital, two people died and five were wounded in renewed fighting between Ethiopian government troops and the Somali Moslem fundamentalist Al-Itihad Al-Islam in the southern Gedo region on Thursday and Friday.

Around 100 Ethiopian troops attacked Gawido village, 10 km (six miles) north of the Bulo Hawo border town, penetrating as far as Surgudud 10 km (six miles) south of Dolow and destroying many houses, according to radio reports monitored in the Somali capital on Saturday.
Al-Itihad commander Colonel Hassan Dahir Aweys said Ethiopian troops, in control of Dolow since clashes last December, attacked his positions outside the town.
Al-Itihad has called a "Jihad" or holy war against Ethiopian forces which thrust into southwest Somalia last month.
Earlier this month an alliance of faction leaders excluding Aideed urged the group to refrain from violence.
